I looked up and saw what I believed to have been the traffic which was a light sport aircraft north of the gap and above us. My student first noticed the traffic and began turning the aircraft left (north west) and shortly thereafter I heard the G1000's traffic warning and looked up to see an aircraft southbound at approximately our same altitude but slightly offset to the east side of the gap close to the mountains. Taking controls I initially turned left (west) as the traffic as to our right but then shortly after beginning my turn the aircraft turned in our direction southwest bound. This is when I decided to perform an emergency descent and turned away from rising terrain. After descending 500 feet the opposing traffic passed behind us and continued westbound. We continued the gap arrival with no further incident. Additionally, it sounded like the same controller was working both tower and ground frequency at GYR.
ASRSN:2211644.s: A flight instructor and student flying a G1000-equipped aircraft on the Gap Arrival at 2,500 MSL encountered a southbound light sport aircraft near the mountains. The instructor executed an emergency descent of 500 feet to avoid a collision after the opposing traffic turned toward them, noting the controller appeared to be working both tower and ground frequencies.

ASRSN:2211731.n: I was PIC and also pilot-flying for all legs of a trip. We boarded our passengers for the live leg (Part 135) to TEB. The SIC briefed the passengers and confirmed that they intended to hold the infant in their lap for the flight. The safety briefing included instructions on requirements for seat belt use.We were cleared to taxi to runway 25 and ran the taxi and before takeoff checklists as usual. We were departing under IFR and the current weather included snow flurries and a broken to overcast ceiling with clear skies above the cloud layer. I briefed the takeoff and departure with the SIC which included the usual go/no-go decision points and also that we would climb above the clouds and cancel IFR once in VMC above the clouds and proceed under VFR to our destination (TEB).Tower instructed us to line-up-and-wait on runway 25 and advised that we were waiting for Departure Control to accept us after the jet that had departed before us had reached 5000' MSL. During this time the SIC again asked the passengers if they had their seat belts fastened as instructed during the safety briefing. The SIC said that they confirmed that their seat belts were fastened.We were cleared for takeoff and to climb on runway heading to 5000' MSL. We then took off and began a normal departure climb. After takeoff the SIC began the 'After Takeoff' checklist. I was hand-flying the aircraft and then engaged the autopilot as we were climbing through approximately 1000' MSL. The SIC then said 'go right, turn right' and instructed me to fly through a hole in the cloud layer. He then called Departure Control and cancelled IFR and asked to proceed VFR to our destination at 12500'. We were still below the cloud layer at this point and I was confused by his instructions to make a right turn to fly through the hole as this was not what we briefed and there was no obvious reason for me to do this.I was still in the process of configuring the plane for the climb. The SIC again said to turn right so I moved the heading bug to initiate a right turn. Shortly thereafter we hit severe-extreme turbulence. This was one solid jolt where the plane was momentarily uncontrollable and everything in the cockpit (soda cans, phones, iPads, etc.) hit the ceiling. I believe I disconnected the autopilot shortly before we encountered the turbulence or shortly thereafter. I was attempting to regain control of the aircraft and we got an over speed alarm several times as we were leveling off and within 10-15 KIAS of Vmo which is 260 KIAS below 8000' MSL. Everything in the cabin that wasn't secure also hit the ceiling. This included the passengers as they had apparently either unfastened or loosened their seat belts even though the 'fasten seat belt' sign was still illuminated. Once I had regained control of the aircraft the SIC went into the cabin to check on the passengers and then to get things cleaned up.During the time the SIC was in the cabin I was configuring the aircraft for the remainder of the climb to 12500' MSL and direct ALB (as instructed by ATC).Upon returning to the cockpit the SIC said that the passengers had some bumps but were otherwise ok and uninjured. The SIC then asked why I didn't turn right immediately and fly through the hole in the clouds and I said that we had not briefed that and that I didn't see a good reason to do it immediately. We then had a brief heated discussion and I then said that I was not going to discuss it further until after we landed and that we were going to concentrate on flying the remainder of the flight.After the flight the SIC said he had received a call that the passengers were claiming they were injured. There was some discussion between them regarding the safety briefing, etc. and apparently the passengers later decided that they were fine and dropped any claim of injury.Initially we thought we may have encountered turbulence related to the clouds and snow showers but after some thought the SICsaid he believed we had encountered the previously departed aircraft's wake. This makes sense to me as well.After taking some time to reflect upon this situation, I believe that I reacted to the SIC command to fly through the hole in the clouds in error. I should have continued to fly the departure as briefed. The SIC has nearly 20,000 hours of pilot time and many more hours in the CE-525 than I do (I was below 100 hrs PIC in the CE-525 at the time of this flight and still on Initial Operating Experience and 'High-Minimums') and is more comfortable doing such maneuvers in the aircraft than I am. I believe the fact that he has much more experience played a role in me attempting to comply with his instructions. As PIC, I should have been firm in refusing to follow the SIC instructions to fly through the hole in the clouds and continued the departure as briefed. It isn't possible to know if this would have resulted in avoiding the severe-extreme turbulence encounter but I believe it would have been the correct action and likely would have avoided the aircraft over speed alarm.
ASRSN:2211731.s: The PIC and SIC of a CE-525 encountered severe turbulence and an overspeed alarm shortly after takeoff when the PIC deviated from the briefed departure to follow the SIC's instruction to fly through a cloud hole. The crew attributed the event to wake turbulence from a preceding jet, while the PIC admitted to error in complying with the SIC's unauthorized maneuver due to the SIC's greater experience.

ASRSN:2211739.n: We Aircraft X a C172 were performing a landing to a full stop on runway XX at ZZZ. The runway was clear as we descended from final to landing. As we touched down and began to apply brakes we heard a radio call from the aircraft holding short of runway XX asking the Aircraft Y landing if they saw the other aircraft (me) on the runway. His response was yes. He performed a landing on a 4700 ft runway that we were only about 1/2 of the way down, still fully on the runway at a slow speed. He was maybe under 1000 ft behind us and should have gone around, not landing. The offending aircraft was Aircraft Y a blue and white single engine aircraft.
ASRSN:2211739.s: A C172 landing on runway XX at ZZZ was followed by Aircraft Y, a single-engine plane, which landed only 1,000 feet behind while the C172 was still occupying half the runway. The reporter states Aircraft Y should have executed a go-around instead of landing.

ASRSN:2211748.n: Landing on Alton Bay Ice runway B18 and just touching down in an experimental light sport. Full flaps and landing 3 point so speed was down near the mid 30 mph range. Just as we were in landing attitude, an adjacent helicopter lifted off on the nearby parallel taxiway. Because we were adjacent, I was caught directly in the full force of their rotor wash. The right wing was lifted pushing us towards the side of the runway. I added power to perform a go around. Since my speed had carried me just beyond the helicopter, the rotorwash from the direct right side was now a tailwind. This took away what little lift I had gained (I was still near full stall and about to land) and prevented the plane from becoming airborne. It then contacted a snowbank which collapsed the left main gear causing the propeller to impact the snow. We came to rest shortly thereafter. There were no injuries to myself or the passenger.
ASRSN:2211748.s: A pilot flying an experimental light sport aircraft on Alton Bay Ice runway B18 encountered severe rotor wash from a departing helicopter during landing. The wash caused a go-around failure and a snowbank impact that collapsed the left main gear and damaged the propeller, though no injuries occurred.

ASRSN:2211750.n: During the vector to approach at 3k feet, approach informs us of the runway closer to spray, I informed him due to ice accumulation we need to come in for landing now or get back to altitude. He responded are you [Advising ATC], I declined it and informed him that we just need the vehicles to move/wait with 12k feet of runway we didn't need anything prepped due to the capabilities of the airplane. He then responded okay I'm [Advising ATC] for you. Gave me the heading to intercept and then cleared us for the approach. We continued flying inbound and switched to tower quickly. They informed us to continue inbound there's a vehicle on the runway while also calling out time remain to, The vehicle to get off the runway. Once we got down under the cloud deck approx 5-600ft we saw the runway and truck on the runway confirming it was just 1. Do to the increasing ice accumulation on the air frame we were committed to landing. Tower called the missed approach twice I replied unable and then said we have the truck in sight we are landing after them, he mentioned that was at my own risk. The truck was off the runway by the time.We touched down and the were on the approach between 500fters and end of runway. Upon landing we noticed the barking action was 4/4/4 and both concluded there was no reason for them to be on the runway. During the post flight we noted the ice was starting to build aft of the protected area. Aircraft X was 15miles south west of FWA on vectors for ILS RW5 at 030MSL.I was informed by tower that the airport has closed the airport due to snow/ice removal.I informed tower that Aircraft X had picked up moderate ice, which he reported in the descent. Aircraft X needed to land and could not hold as requested from the airport ops.I then went back to the pilot asked him if he would like to [Request Priority Handling], due to ice, so he could land. He told me he would if it wasn't for the paperwork. I then choose to issue for him due to safety concerns with the ice accumulation and cleared him onto the approach for ILS5. I then told tower he was an [requesting priority handling] and gave them fuel and souls.I then told Aircraft X to contact tower once he was established onto the approach.Prior to airport ops closing the airport the condition codes were reported at 3/3/3 20% ice 80% wet. Recommendation: I would recommend that the airport ops come up with better procedures, and not close runways when condition codes are within limits for pilots to land. I would also recommend the airport ops go through training on the effect ice accumulation has on airplanes. Also not to assume all aircraft have the ability to hold in icing conditions. I would also recommend not to just forcing runways to close just because they are going to be on it. Work with the tower and clear off the runway when we have an arrival or departure.
ASRSN:2211750.s: A pilot flying Aircraft X encountered moderate ice accumulation while vectored for ILS RW5 at 3,000 feet MSL. Despite the airport closing for snow removal, the controller issued priority handling, allowing the pilot to land safely after a truck cleared the runway, though the pilot criticized the airport's closure procedures.

ASRSN:2211754.n: Taxied on the taxiway parallel to Runway XX to the north end and completed the takeoff checklist while pointing 050 degrees heading. Turned onto the short taxiway at the north end of the runway and taxied to the hold short line for Runway XX. Checked for aircraft traffic and saw no one approaching. After taxiing onto Runway XX, heard another aircraft report short final for Runway XX. We were already rolling. The other aircraft reported abandoning the landing and going around. We never saw the other aircraft. I believe the pilot in our left seat was unable to see the landing aircraft because the Cessna 172 high wing blocked the view up the landing glide path.The pilot had told me he planned to do a complete circle on the ground before taxiing onto the runway, but another aircraft had come up behind us and the pilot flying our airplane judged it to be too tight a turn to do the circle.
ASRSN:2211754.s: The pilot of a Cessna 172 taxied onto Runway XX while another aircraft was on short final, forcing that aircraft to go around. The reporter attributed the runway incursion to the high-wing blocking the left-seat pilot's view and the decision to skip a planned ground circle due to traffic behind.

ASRSN:2211761.n: I had checked weather and filed IFR for my flight home a couple of hours prior to my arrival. Approximately 40 minutes out from landing I was checking weather and noticed ceiling had come down some but was still above approach mins. I setup my avionics for the runway with the lowest minimums approach and requested vectors. Upon descent thru the clouds on the approach I started to pickup the lights of the runway and when I finally saw clearly them I realized I was lower than I expected. After landing I figured out I had incorrectly set my minimums and ended up being around 200' low when I broke out. I have a lot of time in this airplane and complacency is a very real threat that bit me on this one.
ASRSN:2211761.s: The pilot, while conducting an IFR approach in an aircraft with significant experience, broke out of clouds approximately 200 feet below the intended minimums. The incident was caused by the pilot incorrectly setting the minimums in the avionics due to complacency.

ASRSN:2211775.n: Aircraft X checked in on a legacy RNAV arrival into ZZZ. told aircraft to turn 10 degrees right during a turn and maintain 140. They said they were in a turn a requested heading. they read back 140. I said present heading maintain 140. they read back present heading 140. I observed the aircraft descending through 136. I gave the altimeter and told them to climb to 140. They said they were instructed to descend to 130. I told them to climb to 140 again. The lowest altitude I observed was 132 in a 140 MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). I think the aircraft had expectation bias knowing the arrival controllers usually descend aircraft to 130 even though I said and they read back 140.Recommendation: issue low altitude alert to aircraft instead of just telling them to climb.
ASRSN:2211775.s: An air traffic controller observed Aircraft X descend to 132 feet below the 140 MVA during a legacy RNAV arrival. The controller attributed the deviation to pilot expectation bias regarding standard descent clearances, despite correct readbacks of the 140-foot instruction.

ASRSN:2211782.n: We were taxiing out at DEN on a windy day. At one point nearly all flights were departing 25 for the winds, but they were starting to die down as we pushed. We had planned for 25 but were assigned 34L. We worked on the runway change while taxiing, but we were also waiting on final weights due to 'an illegal load limit.' We were given a taxi via WB and D, and we informed tower that we were waiting on our numbers while on D. We were told to hold short of D2, which we did while waiting for the final weights. The final weights popped up right as tower told us to taxi a box pattern around (Runway 34L, D3, D hold short D2) to let traffic behind us pass. I informed tower we had our weights and would be good to go in a minute, and he acknowledged that and verified he still wanted us to taxi around. Entering the weights also required manually entering the V speeds since we were using Max T/O with reduced V speeds due to the gusty crosswind, and also it took a second to verify the new runway was loaded correctly with no discontinuities since it had been loaded while taxiing. As a result we were halfway through the before takeoff checklist as we taxied back onto D and Tower cleared us to line up and wait 34L. I said we need just 30 seconds (as we were finishing the checklist at that time) and Tower said in an annoyed tone there's people behind you". I'll admit the comment took me aback, so I just said 'just a few more seconds' and he responded with 'yeah right.' We were still taxiing toward the runway slowly so that we'd have the checklist completed before we got to the hold short line, and so we were just about to enter the WA/D intersection when Tower cleared Aircraft Y on WA to line up and wait. We slammed on the brakes, but our nose was in the intersection. He then told us to pass behind Aircraft Y, but at that point it wouldn't have been safe for Aircraft Y to taxi past. Tower then said 'Aircraft X, did you just cut Aircraft Y off without clearance?' and I responded 'It was our understanding that we had clearance to the runway.' Tower then said that there was more room on Aircraft Y EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time) anyway and cleared us for takeoff.It is possible that I misheard or simply missed a call, but it was my understanding that we were not holding short of WA. I acknowledge that I certainly might have missed a call at that point as we were entering weights and V-speeds, verifying everything was in the box correctly for the gusty T/O and runway change, running the checklist, and dealing with Tower's comments over the radio all adding to the task saturation." Taxiing out 34L at DEN advised ground we were negative weights. Tower cleared us D short of D2. About the time weights came he gave us D WA 34L D3 & hold short of D2 (just a box around). We told him weights were coming and he replied he still needed us follow that clearance. After we boxed around ground told us to line up & wait 34L. Due to some issues being resolved in our FMC, we were late getting our checklists complete & were going to need another minute. The tower's response to us was 'yeah sure.' As we approached WA he cleared a Aircraft Y's flight onto 34L. I immediately stopped but the nose of the airplane was on WA. Tower said our clearance was to hold short of D2. Aircraft Y responded he could still get by but tower told him he needed spacing (or something like that) for him anyway. Tower cleared us for takeoff & we took the runway & departed.
ASRSN:2211782.s: Pilots taxiing a Boeing at Denver International Airport experienced task saturation while resolving weight and runway changes, leading to a runway incursion where the nose entered intersection WA. Air Traffic Control initially cleared the aircraft to hold short of D2 but later cleared another aircraft onto the runway, resulting in a stop and subsequent takeoff clearance.

ASRSN:2211787.n: In cruise FL370 approximately 9 hours after takeoff, 150 NM northwest of YBR, in radar contact with Winnipeg Control we received a clearance to fly direct to BRNDN intersection which is on our route and part of the GIBBZ5 STAR. Approximately 100 NM later we were switched to a different Winnipeg sector and after checking in he asked us to what point we were cleared to and we answered by spelling" BRNDN. He laughed and said that they had intended to clear us to Brandon VOR YBR... NOT BRNDN intersection. I reloaded the FMC direct YBR and rebuilt our route back to original. We asked if there was any loss of separation and he said NO." Winnipeg Center cleared us direct to a fix. We heard and went direct to fix BRNDN." A while later a different Winnipeg Controller queried us about our clearance. We told him we were going direct "BRNDN." He then cleared us direct to the NAVAID "Brandon" (YBR). So there was confusion, since there were two fixes pronounced the same but spelled differently."
ASRSN:2211787.s: Pilots in cruise at FL370 flew direct to the BRNDN intersection instead of the intended Brandon VOR (YBR) due to a controller's ambiguous clearance. The crew corrected the route after a second controller clarified the confusion between the two similarly pronounced fixes, with no loss of separation reported.

ASRSN:2211789.n: During this flight we were on the RNAV Runway 7 approach. RAIM was good and all procedures followed. When we broke out of clouds and saw the runway we determined we were HIGH YET VNAV PATH showed us 500 feet LOW. We absolutely weren't not LOW and the VNAV PATH was unreliable. The ILS was not a factor for this approach and a new ILS being installed doesn't solve the problem of something wrong with the VNAV path. Last month I shared the experience and have been told that GPS spoofing is becoming an issue. I am concerned that is what happened to us on Day 0 in SPN.
ASRSN:2211789.s: The flight crew on an RNAV Runway 7 approach observed a VNAV path discrepancy showing 500 feet low while visually high. The pilot attributed the unreliable VNAV guidance to potential GPS spoofing, noting that the new ILS installation does not address this specific issue.

ASRSN:2211803.n: After pushback, after Start checklist during recall check, master caution FLT CTRL pushed, auto slat light came on. Talked to Maintenance Control and deferred light. Received a new release and continued operation. After takeoff SPD LIM flags appeared on Captain's FLT director. Crew QRH Unreliable Airspeed checklist and continued since First Officer's (FO's) FLT director was good. Roughly at FL250 the Captain's 'stick shaker' went off. The crew decided to return to ZZZ and spoke to Maintenance Control and Dispatcher. We also decided to land overweight about 10,000 lbs. The FO made an ILS XXL approach to a smooth landing since his FLT director was working. We [requested priority handling] as a precaution but the emergency vehicles were not needed. Taxied on our own to gate XX. After push back and after start checklist recall check, master caution flight control and autoslat fail light were illuminated. The crew spoke to Dispatcher and Maintenance Control, we deferred it, got a new release, continued the operation. After take off, SPD LIM flag appeared on Captain side only. The crew ran Airspeed Unreliable Airspeed QRH And started communicating with the Dispatcher and Maintenance Control. The stick shaker on Captain side went off. The crew decided to return to ZZZ and communicated with passengers, flight attendants, Maintenance Control, Dispatcher and more.The crew decided overweight landing to prevent further system failure in timely manner. Also [priority handling was requested].The crew safely landed overweight via ILS XXL and parked at XX gate on power.
ASRSN:2211803.s: The crew deferred a flight control and auto slat light after pushback, then encountered Captain-side SPD LIM flags and stick shaker activation after takeoff. They returned to ZZZ for an overweight ILS XXL landing using the First Officer's functional flight director, requesting priority handling but requiring no emergency vehicles.

ASRSN:2211804.n: While climbing in day IMC conditions, the Captain side window 1 had a bright glowing spot. It was roughly the size of a dime and the light intensity was about that of the sun. We [requested priority handling] and requested to land at ZZZ as we had just left and were not far. The light dimmed and became a glowing melted ball of window material. There was never smoke on the inside of the flight deck. We tried to contact company via the call me function but were too low for the frequency. Unable to raise dispatch on VHF and nearing ZZZ, I sent a quick ACARS text to Dispatch. We landed and were met by emergency vehicles who said they couldn't see an unusual heat signature on the outside of the aircraft. We taxied to the gate.
ASRSN:2211804.s: During a climb in day IMC, the Captain observed a bright glowing spot on window 1 that melted into a ball. The crew requested priority handling, landed at ZZZ, and taxied to the gate after emergency vehicles reported no external heat signature.

ASRSN:2211817.n: De-iced at ZZZ de-ice pad. The aircraft sat overnight and had at least 4' of snow and ice everywhere. Iceman had us shut down both engines and said they would de-ice gear, engines, wings, tail, and fuselage and then apply type 4. At completion we were told 'post check complete' and recorded the time etc. Upon arrival at ZZZ1 found packed snow and ice in the L and R main landing gear on walk around. This forced us to get de-iced again in ZZZ1 which would NOT have been necessary had ZZZ de-iced properly.
ASRSN:2211817.s: The flight crew reported that after overnight de-icing at ZZZ, packed snow and ice remained on the main landing gear upon arrival at ZZZ1. This required a second de-icing at ZZZ1, which the crew attributed to improper de-icing procedures at the initial station.

ASRSN:2211828.n: I was operating as First Officer and pilot monitoring on our flight into ZZZ. On short final, around 500 feet, tower issued a go-around for traffic not clearing the runway quickly enough. We executed the go-around per SOP and complied with ATC instructions. The flight continued normally and successfully to our destination.
ASRSN:2211828.s: The First Officer reported that on short final at 500 feet into ZZZ, ATC issued a go-around due to traffic not clearing the runway. The crew executed the maneuver per SOP, and the flight continued normally to the destination.

ASRSN:2211866.n: We were setup for and briefed the SNDIA 4 RNAV Arrival followed by the RNAV (RNP) Y Rwy 21. About 30 NM from ABQ airport approach control gave a heading to fly and said to expect the visual approach Rwy 21. I elected to use the final portion of the briefed RNAV approach as reference for the visual approach. We were cleared for the visual approach at an approximately 5 NM right base for Rwy 21. I did not set TDZE in the altitude window and selected Approach instead of utilizing LNAV/VNAV. Without benefit of reasonable flight director guidance, I descended to approximately 6400 feet (1000 feet AGL) as I was visually maneuvering to wings level on final. When rolling wings level I recognized I was not in a good position to land (low on PAPI, otherwise stable) from this approach and initiated a Go Around. Tower called soon after Go Around initiation to give a low altitude warning. The Go Around was uneventful and we were vectored for another visual approach to Rwy 21 that culminated in a successful landing.If I was in the same situation again I would initiate the Go Around sooner. I know that I was behind on this approach. Though I was comfortable that the aircraft was visibly clear of obstacles on final, I allowed myself to descend to 1000 feet AGL too far from the Runway. I didn't have much time to discuss, once we were told to expect the visual approach, but I could have done more to prepare for a successful approach. I told the FO that I would utilize the RNAV for reference. But, I should have also reiterated how I intended to use LNAV/VNAV and would remove Baro mins from the PFD and set TDZE instead.
ASRSN:2211866.s: The pilot flying a visual approach to Runway 21 at ABQ descended to 6,400 feet without setting TDZE or using LNAV/VNAV, resulting in a low position on the PAPI. The crew initiated a go-around after receiving a low altitude warning from Tower and subsequently completed a successful landing on a second attempt.

ASRSN:2211869.n: Upon landing, the Tower gave us the entire taxi of Taxiway F, S, T while on rollout of the runway. I was focused on completing the landing on the runway and exiting the nearest taxiway upon rollout. I was looking outside for our taxiways after Person A and I agreed on the taxi route. Person A and I could almost see nothing at all in terms of taxiways due to an extreme lack of lighting. I was taxiing very slowly because something did not feel right. I then stopped because I noticed what looked to be a much larger taxiway roughly 15 feet ahead of us so I stopped. At the same moment, the Tower said we missed our turn and we had entered a runway. However, we did not. We then asked for a progressive taxi at least 3 times before the controller would respond.Cause: Almost no lighting on taxiways as well as very faint paint. And that's in addition to it being night with rain. Suggestions: Increased lighting and improved paint on the taxiways at OPF.
ASRSN:2211869.s: The pilot reported that poor lighting and faint paint at night caused a runway incursion risk while taxiing at OPF. The crew stopped before entering a runway after the Tower incorrectly stated they had missed their turn, prompting requests for progressive taxi instructions.

ASRSN:2211871.n: After landing at ZZZZ the right brake temp indicator was showing a 6. After confirming with ground crew that the aircraft was chocked it was decided we would release the parking brake to allow the brakes to cool. While running through the before start checklist, the 'parking brake set' line item was read and responded without actual verification. The parking brake was not set. After accomplishing both engine starts, both pilots were heads down in the cockpit accomplishing after start flows. I looked up and realized the aircraft was rolling uncomanded I quickly stepped on the brakes and altered the pic that we were rolling. The aircraft came to a stop and the parking brake was set. The aircraft had only rolled about 3 feet and was not in contact with anything around us. A Marshaller was standing in front of the aircraft but was still 10-15 feet away from the nose. As a crew we decided to run the before start checklist again as well as the after start checklist to ensure nothing else was missed. We talked about the reason for the Parking brake not being set and took a safety time out to ensure we were both okay to continue. Remainder of the flight continued without issue.
ASRSN:2211871.s: The flight crew released the parking brake to cool brakes after landing but failed to verify it was set during the before start checklist. The aircraft rolled uncommanded about three feet while both pilots were distracted, stopping safely after the pilot applied brakes and set the parking brake.

ASRSN:2211879.n: During flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ on Day 0, we encountered a bleed leak and multiple anti-icing failures while in IMC and icing conditions. The surrounding airspace remained IMC throughout the flight, and icing began during descent.At 4,100 feet, as we approached the final approach fix, we received EICAS messages: Bleed Low Temp, Anti-Ice Low Capacity, Wing Anti-Ice Fail, and Anti-Ice Inop. The Captain increased thrust and extended the gear to increase drag, but near the final approach fix, a bleed leak warning appeared. Given the continuous IMC and active snowfall, the fastest way to exit icing conditions was to land as soon as possible.After [requesting priority handling] for safety, we conducted a normal landing. I ran the Bleed Leak QRH while the Captain coordinated with ATC and the Flight Attendant. Fire trucks were on standby and inspected the aircraft, finding no visible issues. We then taxied to the gate, where maintenance was called, and the aircraft was written up.
ASRSN:2211879.s: The crew encountered a bleed leak and multiple anti-icing failures in IMC icing conditions during descent to ZZZ. They landed normally after requesting priority handling; fire trucks inspected the aircraft with no visible issues, and maintenance was called at the gate.

ASRSN:2211881.n: I was operating flight ABCD on Day 0. Thunderstorms in the vicinity of ZZZ airport shut down ramp operations and we were waiting inside the aircraft for conditions to improve. Once the ramp opened up, my First Officer (FO) performed a walk-around and was informed that high winds had shifted the jet bridge and we should have maintenance take a look to ensure nothing had been damaged. I went back into the flight deck to contact maintenance to perform an inspection, alongside one other minor maintenance item.While I was writing up the report, I heard two sharp bangs on the fuselage of the aircraft. I went out to investigate and was informed that the jetbridge had struck the fuselage.I followed up by contacting Dispatch, station leads and various other members of the team to rectify the situation, and ultimately ended up deplaning the aircraft once it was confirmed safe to do so.Suggestions: I would suggest ground personnel responsible for operating the jetbridge review protocol for dealing with a situation in which the bridge is shifted by high winds.
ASRSN:2211881.s: The Captain of flight ABCD reported that high winds shifted a jet bridge at ZZZ airport, causing it to strike the aircraft fuselage while the crew waited for ramp operations to resume. The incident resulted in a maintenance inspection and the subsequent deplaning of passengers once the aircraft was confirmed safe.

ASRSN:2211884.n: After getting deiced in the Central Deicing Facility (CDF) we were given instructions to taxi to XXL. We let Tower know that we needed 30 second run up on runway due to the conditions outside. They said to inform when we were ready to roll. Advanced thrust to 40% then 70%. After about 2-3 second cockpit started to fill with white/gray smoke. Pulled throttles back to idle. We ran QRC for smoke and fumes and had Tower deploy Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF). Flight Attendants (FAs) called up and said smoke in cabin. Lav smoke detector also went off. Ran QRH. Had ARFF check out aircraft for fire outside which they did not see. Smoke dissipated quickly so we decided to taxi back with ARFF following us since no indication inside or out of fire. ARFF came onboard at gate with heat detecting gun but found no fire indication inside.Cause: We believe it may have been deice fluid that got into engine. Pre-flight and taxi out were normal. We briefed the de ice and engine runup requirements at the gate. The taxiways were quite snowy.We taxied to the Central Deicing Facility (CDF) and configured for de ice with the APU off and engines running. We asked for Type I entire aircraft and Type IV on the wings and tail. After completion we ran the reconfiguration checklist and proceeded to exit the CDF. We advised Ground Control on initial contact after de-ice of our need to perform a 30 second runup on the runway prior to takeoff roll. We were initially given XXL [Intersection] 1 for departure. While taxiing they changed our departure to full length behind a Boeing 777. We doubled back and while stopped we proceeded to extend the flaps and do the checklist. We then awaited further clearance. We were told to line up and wait and then given permission to do our runup. I stopped on centerline and gave controls to the First Officer (FO). I assumed pilot monitoring (PM) duties and ATC told us to let them know when we were ready to roll. No takeoff clearance was given. I acknowledged and the FO increased thrust to 40% (stabilized) and then proceeded to increase thrust to 70% where I then began the timer. During this time I noticed a haze/smoke in the cockpit. I notified the FO and we brought the thrust levers back to idle. I assumed pilot flying (PF) duties again and called for the Smoke/Fire/Fumes checklist in the QRC. I notified ATC we couldn't continue and had smoke in the cockpit. Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) was requested. The smoke/haze began to dissipate after the thrust levers were brought to idle. The Flight Attendants then called and said they saw the smoke/haze and the forward lavatory smoke detector began to go off. The smoke/haze was throughout the cabin but more concentrated in the forward half of the aircraft. No flames were seen. The FO continued the checklist in the QRH. While trying to communicate with ARFF that we needed the exterior of the aircraft inspected, what the present situation was and continuing the checklist we had constant calls from the Flight Attendants asking if we were going to make a PA, how to turn off the forward lavatory smoke detector and wanting to know what the smoke/haze was. I told them several times we were trying to complete the checklist and made sure they and the passengers were okay. I told them I would make a PA about the situation when we had our thoughts straight about what was happening. The checklist was completed and I then made a PA to the passengers stating that the smoke/haze was dissipating, safety vehicles were approaching the aircraft to inspect the exterior as a precaution and then they would escort us back to the gate. I said we believed the smoke was from de ice fluid that made its way into the engines. At some point during this the forward lavatory smoke detector stopped sounding. We taxied back to the gate normally. Upon reaching the gate I made a PA that firefighters were entering the aircraft to use a thermal heat device in the lavatory to ensure everything was okay. Once finished I made a PA from the galley phone instructing everybody to please gather all belongings and exit the aircraft.The smoke was a white/grey color with a smell I have never smelled. The flight attendants thought it smelled electrical in nature but neither the FO or I thought that's what it was. We believed it was de ice fluid burning from engine intake.Cause: The airport conditions were snow covered taxiways with active snow. This risk was mitigated with a slower taxi speed and de ice. We had a runway change from XXL 1 to XXL full length. We already had takeoff numbers for the intersection takeoff so we only had to mitigate the risk of new taxi instructions and snow covered taxiways.The constant calls from the Flight Attendants asking the same question several times while trying to complete a checklist and speak with ARFF was very task saturating. This could be mitigated by preparing Captain's more for situations where they get constant calls during emergency situations.
ASRSN:2211884.s: During a pre-takeoff engine runup on a snow-covered runway, the flight crew experienced white smoke in the cockpit and cabin, likely caused by deicing fluid entering the engines. The crew aborted the takeoff, completed emergency checklists, and taxied back to the gate with ARFF escort after no fire was detected.

ASRSN:2211886.n: After leaving the CDF (Central Deice Facility) and being told to expect XXL they changed runways on us and wanted us to taxi to XYR. The instructions they gave us were to taxi on [Taxiway] 1 and hold short 2. As we were taxiing down 1 to hold short of 2 Captain mentioned he was having trouble stopping aircraft and let Ground know we would go past 2 due to poor braking as the taxiway in this area looked fairly bad. Once passing 2 taxiway looked much cleaner and we were told to keep taxiing on 1 to 3 and do a U turn to join 3 and 4 to taxi towards XYR. As we are taxiing at minimal speed Captain mentions he has brakes fully pressed in trying to stop but nothing is happening and we had no skidding/sliding going on. At this point I joined the Captain on the brakes and press them fully in with no stop either. Aircraft came to a stop about 10 seconds in total after. Other aircraft infront of us did not report issue with taxiway and ATIS did not state poor conditions on taxiway. At this point we were afraid to keep going as we did not know if we had a brake issue and we were going to ZZZ1 which is short runway. We also did not know if deicing fluid got in the brakes. We felt the safe decision was to return to gate with a tow as we did not want to not be able to not stop and go off the taxiway or hit something. Wrote plane up at gate. Cause: Taxiways were not reported to have poor conditions. Aircraft infront of us did not report poor braking or issues. We felt we had a brake issue going on and did not want to risk going off the taxiway or hitting something so we made the safe call to stop and get a tow to gate.
ASRSN:2211886.s: The flight crew experienced ineffective braking while taxiing from the deicing facility to runway XYR, despite no reported poor conditions. Suspecting a brake failure or fluid contamination, they safely returned to the gate for a tow and wrote up the aircraft.

ASRSN:2211901.n: Taxi in from landing to Gate XX. Spots depicted on JEPPS are completely wrong. We almost taxied down alley beyond point of turning around. We were actually going to a hardstand (we were unaware) and did not see rampers positioned at a completely different location. The numbered spots at the airport DO NOT correlate to those on our JEPPS Page 10-9A for PVR (MMPR). Cause: Incorrect information published on JEPPS. Correct diagram on Page 10-9A PVR to correspond with actual airport spot numbers.
ASRSN:2211901.s: The flight crew taxiing to Gate XX at PVR nearly entered a hardstand because Jeppesen chart spot numbers did not match actual airport markings. The incident was caused by incorrect published information on Jeppesen Page 10-9A, which failed to correlate with real ramp locations.

ASRSN:2211941.n: While on Taxiway 1, in ZZZ in nighttime, snowy conditions on contaminated surfaces, we ended up becoming number 4 in line due to a disabled aircraft that required a tow off the taxiway and back to a gate. We and the other aircraft sat for over 45 minutes with both engines running due to slick airport surfaces, where braking action was less than good. When the line on Taxiway 1 started to move again, it started off fine, however, there was one point where the aircraft in front of us came to a stop. I applied brakes and thought that this was taking longer to stop than normal. I pressed harder on the full brakes and nothing was happening. At this point, I realized that we were, in fact, sliding towards the 737 in front of us. Unable to stop, I thought that it would be safer to try to turn the aircraft towards the left edge of the taxiway and possibly slide off the pavement instead of into another aircraft. I slowly began to turn the tiller thinking if I aggressively turned we would've continued to slide forward. I also applied the parking brake. The aircraft began to turn and slide in both directions forward and towards the edge of the taxiway, but came to a stop a few feet before the edge of Taxiway 1. My FO reported on Ground that [we] were sliding and eventually came to a stop, the aircraft in front of us at that time began to slowly move forward. We never left the taxi surface. When we had enough spacing, I was able to release the brake and slowly align the aircraft back up with centerline and continue taxiing.
ASRSN:2211941.s: Pilots taxiing a jet on contaminated Taxiway 1 at ZZZ at night lost braking effectiveness while following a stopped aircraft. They steered the sliding aircraft toward the taxiway edge to avoid a collision, stopping safely on the pavement before resuming the taxi.

ASRSN:2211948.n: During the encounter phase of flight the left engine shut down, the FADAC restarted the engine after the APU came on line. This happened an additional two times and then the engine to operate normally.Suggestions: No idea that would be a maintenance question.
ASRSN:2211948.s: During the encounter phase, the left engine shut down three times before operating normally after the APU came online and the FADAC restarted it. The pilot reported no known cause and suggested the issue was a maintenance question.

ASRSN:2211985.n: Taxi out, fume odor, captain called flight attendants to verify if observed, it was confirmed that we had odor, taste in mouth, of fuel.Captain reports aircraft history of fume events. After successfully starting both engines using APU BLEED and selecting the APU BLEED PB to OFF a very strong odor immediately filled the flightdeck. I conferred with all FLIGHT ATTENDANTS via interphone and all FAs reported smelling a very strong odor. Odor is described as a fume from vaporized/aerosolized engine oil. It was not fire, electrical, deice fluid or fuel. FO and I jointly coordinated an expeditious return to gate XX and deplaned passengers into the airport terminal via jetway. All crewmembers were removed from duty. Based on my physical symptoms after the event and on the advice of medical, I went to ER for evaluation. This aircraft has a known history of SMOKE ODOR FUME event in the previous 30 days that sent multiple crewmembers and passengers to seek medical treatment.Industry needs to figure out prevention of these dangerous events.
ASRSN:2211985.s: During taxi out, the flight crew and cabin crew detected a strong engine oil fume odor after turning off the APU bleed. The aircraft returned to the gate, passengers deplaned, and all crew were removed from duty, with the captain seeking medical evaluation for symptoms.

ASRSN:2211994.n: Immediately upon takeoff from ZZZ, a strong odor permeated the cabin. At first it smelled like exhaust fumes, then escalated to the smell of burning fuel, then burning plastic. FA2 (Flight Attendant 2) and myself, FA4, were seated in the back and got up to feel the lavatory doors for heat in case there was a fire. None was felt, so we looked inside and found neither smoke nor flames. In fact, the trash compartments in both lavs had popped open on takeoff so it was easy to see there was no issue inside the lavatories. The smoke detector in the forward lavatory then went off. I saw the FA1 and FA3 check that lavatory and decided to grab the PPE and halon extinguisher and head up front just in case they needed it immediately. There was no smoke or flames present in the forward lavatory either, however the odor was still strong throughout the cabin. The Captain called about the lavatory smoke detector and after a quick discussion, told us that we would be returning to ZZZ and back to the Gate. He made an announcement to the passengers, we prepared the cabin for landing, and we landed about 10 minutes later. The entire flight lasted about 20 minutes. The odor did not dissipate until after we landed. The entire crew reported headaches and feeling dizzy. Three of us removed ourselves from the flight.
ASRSN:2211994.s: Flight attendants reported strong odors of exhaust, burning fuel, and plastic immediately after takeoff from ZZZ, triggering a forward lavatory smoke detector. The Captain returned to the gate within 20 minutes; the odor persisted until landing, causing headaches and dizziness that led three crew members to remove themselves from duty.

ASRSN:2212011.n: On Day 0, me and a partner were assigned to install borescope plugs on Aircraft X. My partner accomplished installation of borescope plugs C, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L and M, I double checked his installation instructions and everything was done in accordance with Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) 72-00-00-290-804. I stamped the checked by block on the task card.Cause: We worked off the maintenance manual step I(2) for installing just the borescope plugs, there was no job card used. As a side note the plugs we installed we're on the inboard side core cowl, the crank pad on this engine is located outboard side fan cowl, we left the engine open because there was more work to accomplished.Suggestions: A separate item should have been made from the beginning that the crank pad was removed. Next time we will read the next step on the paperwork to determine if any thing else needs to be documented. On Day 0, I along with a partner was assigned to install 9 borescope plugs on Aircraft X. We accomplished the borescope plugs installation and signed of the paperwork in accordance with Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) 72-00-00-290-804. section I-2, The plugs were C, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L and M. The job was accomplished in the hangar. They were more work to be accomplished on open items.Cause: There wasn't a work card used for this job. We used the maintenance manual and we were working from the task card items which only call for the borescope plugs. Suggestions: An item should have been created for removal of the crank pad cover which would have been our indication to reinstall the crank pad cover. Next time I will read further into the paperwork and make sure that the next step has been documented to be accomplished.
ASRSN:2212011.s: Two mechanics installed borescope plugs on Aircraft X using AMM 72-00-00-290-804 but failed to document the removal of the crank pad cover because no specific work card existed for that task. The engine was left open for further work, prompting a recommendation to create separate items for cover removal to ensure proper documentation.

ASRSN:2212023.n: Yesterday, me and my First Officer were operating flight ZZZ1 to ZZZ when a missed approach occurred while conducting the ILS XXR. The flight conditions for the last 30 minutes of the flight were filled with moderate to severe turbulence and similar precipitation. Just inside the FAF (ZZZZZ) I got a glide-slope flag on my PFD (Primary Flight Display) followed by a LOC flag. Soon after the flags my flight director disappeared. Pretty soon after my flight director failed my First Officer's PFD reflected the same data (a failed LOC and glide-slope). I then called for a 'go around'. My First Officer slowly brought the power up and we proceeded to do our standardized calls. Although power was brought in, he failed to press the TOGA switches on his side so it never sequenced the missed approach. I proceeded to prompt him to press the buttons so that we could receive the required lateral guidance to commence with the missed approach. While this occurred, we proceeded to get blown off the lateral ground track of the runway by a 45 knot crosswind that was present at 3,500/4,000 feet. After getting instructions by ATC to commence with an immediate right turn, we began to proceed to the right, but it was delayed due to the moderate turbulence and heavy rain that we were experiencing. After getting re-sequenced we came back around and landed normally on XXR.
ASRSN:2212023.s: The Captain and First Officer of flight ZZZ1 experienced ILS glide-slope and localizer failures during the approach in turbulence and rain. The First Officer failed to press TOGA switches, delaying the missed approach sequence while a 45-knot crosswind blew the aircraft off track before ATC vectored them for a normal landing.

ASRSN:2212030.n: On initial approach into Lubbock on ILS 26, navigation showed we were on course, needle was centered. However, Lubbock Tower said were off course by one mile and to make a missed approach. We made missed approach and returned for RNAV Approach 35. Tower again stated we were off course by 1 mile and requested missed approach. However, navigation showed us on course. Another aircraft also in pattern stated they were told the same on ILS 26. Also on ILS 17 another aircraft was told off course but they were not. During this go-around we were having difficulty with autopilot and altitude varied by between 100 - 200 feet. Made missed approach and came back around and landed ILS 17 with no difficulty.
ASRSN:2212030.s: Pilots on initial ILS 26 and RNAV 35 approaches into Lubbock were told by Tower they were one mile off course despite centered navigation, while experiencing autopilot altitude variations of 100–200 feet. After multiple missed approaches, the crew landed safely on ILS 17, noting other aircraft received similar conflicting off-course advisories.

ASRSN:2212033.n: While on final approach, our flight was instructed to perform an immediate go-around due to conflicting tra'c crossing our approach path. This report aims to highlight the risks associated with crossing tra'c in close proximity to aircraft on final approach while fully configured for landing. Phase of Flight: Approach - Final ApproachOur flight was conducting an instrument approach to Runway 33 at MOB, descending from the final approach fix in instrument meteorological conditions and transitioning to visual meteorological conditions. I was the pilot flying. Upon switching to Tower frequency, we received landing clearance. While conducting the landing checklist, the Tower advised us of crossing traffic at our 12 o'clock and requested that we report the tra'c in sight. Both the pilot monitoring and I began scanning for the reported tra'c but were unable to visually acquire it within the first few seconds. Shortly thereafter, Tower issued an immediate instruction to 'Make an immediate left turn, climb 4,000 feet now.' At the same time, our Tra'c Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) displayed a highlighted aircraft at our altitude, approximately one mile ahead. Recognizing the potential conflict, I initiated a go-around and executed a left turn while climbing as instructed. During the maneuver, we visually identified the conflicting tra'c, a helicopter crossing our approach path. The helicopter also initiated a climb. ATC then instructed us to turn to heading 230° and climb to 3,000 feet. We complied, reconfigured the aircraft, and completed all required checklists. We were subsequently resequenced for approach, received another landing clearance, and completed an uneventful landing.Factors Contributing to the Event:- The crossing tra'c was not initially visible despite being reported by Tower.- The immediate nature of the ATC instruction required a rapid response.- The proximity of the conflicting tra'c, combined with our fully configured state for landing, added complexity to the maneuver.- The TCAS did not issue a Resolution Advisory (RA), but the tra'c was displayed as a potential conflict.Safety Concerns & Recommendations:- Enhanced coordination between Approach and Tower controllers to ensure situational awareness regarding crossing tra'c near the final approach course.- Consideration of stricter restrictions on crossing tra'c in close proximity to aircraft on final approach, especially when fully configured for landing.- Review of ATC procedures for issuing timely tra'c advisories to provide crews with better situational awareness.- Further discussion on aircraft unable to hear other military tra'c radio calls within the same airspace.While no aircraft limitations were exceeded, and a TCAS RA was not triggered, this event underscores the potential hazards of crossing tra'c near final approach. I submit this report to promote discussion and reinforce the importance of safe separation between landing aircraftand crossing traffic.
ASRSN:2212033.s: The pilot flying a fully configured aircraft on final approach to MOB Runway 33 executed an immediate go-around after ATC instructed a climb due to a crossing helicopter. The conflict occurred because the helicopter was not initially visible despite ATC advisories, though TCAS displayed the target without issuing a Resolution Advisory.

ASRSN:2212041.n: The student of mine went onto solo flight, and while he return to airport to land he lost directional control after touchdown, he then went straight through the grass and into a taxiway, no person was harmed no damage to the airplane, and no damage done to the field.
ASRSN:2212041.s: A student pilot lost directional control after touchdown during a solo return to the airport, veering through grass onto a taxiway. The incident resulted in no injuries, no aircraft damage, and no damage to the airfield.

ASRSN:2212043.n: While descending via the OZZZI1 arrival we began experiencing St. Elmo's Fire around FL220. At approximately FL200 we experienced a lightning strike on the CA side of the aircraft. All systems were operating normally except for the CA AOA indicator which we performed the ECAM for. Prior to the lightning strike, onboard weather radar didn't indicate any hazardous weather prior to our descent from cruise. During the descent the weather radar began to pick up heavy precipitation. We contacted ATL Center to see if any other aircraft reported ride conditions. They responded that no one had recently. We started to experience moderate turbulence and asked for vectors from ATC. We were told that they were working on bringing us North of the field rather than to the South as published. The aircraft was struck prior to any rerouting. Once rerouted, we landed safely at the field. Aircraft suffered a damaged AOA indicator discovered upon post flight inspection.I believe this incident could have been prevented with better routing from ATC. Vectors to an arrival from the West prior to our descent could have navigated around the weather that we experienced and mitigated the chances of a lightning strike. The Airbus does have weather radar, but is limited with its ability to see the 'bigger picture'.
ASRSN:2212043.s: The flight crew encountered St. Elmo's Fire and a lightning strike on the CA side during descent via the OZZZI1 arrival, damaging the AOA indicator. The pilot attributed the incident to ATC routing that failed to avoid heavy precipitation and turbulence, suggesting earlier vectors from the West would have prevented the strike.

ASRSN:2212052.n: It was a clear cool day with a few cirrus clouds overhead. I started the engine, listened to the ATIS and set my altimeter. I switched to CTAF. I taxied out to the run up area at Runway 31, via Taxiway B. I have dual electronic ignition and accomplished the 'mag' check at low RPM while taxiing as I usually do. I stopped at the run up area. The wind sock at Runway 31 at MTJ showed a very light breeze nearly parallel to the runway. I increased the RPM to 1700 and listened to the engine while the oil temp increased to 110 F. During this time I heard another aircraft announce entering into the pattern. There was also a call from a small aircraft but I was not able to understanding anything other than their make and model. I made visual contact with an aircraft on downwind, a little before abeam midfield for Runway 31, left traffic. I had the engine heater plugged in from the night before and the oil cooler is configured for winter flying so getting to take off oil temp did not take very long. I scanned the pattern visually while turning prior to taxiing onto Runway 31. Again I saw the aircraft I previously saw on downwind, he was turning left base roughly a mile and a half out. I looked for traffic in front of the plane I had a visual with. I saw no other traffic in front of him. I also looked for traffic for Runways 35 and 17 and determined it was clear. I announced that I was taking Runway 31 for a right cross wind departure. I kept talking that I had the aircraft on left downwind in sight and that I was taking off without delay, and that I was looking for the other traffic. Prior to lift off speed, but well into the run, I saw a business class jet taxiing towards the terminal on Taxiway C or D. I would have seen it earlier but it's vertical stab and rudder were painted black. I anticipated he would stop prior to crossing Runway 31. I continued the take off run and was becoming airborne right about the time I realized he wasn't going to stop and right about then he called out that he would be crossing Runway 31. While I was passing over head I radioed him not calmly, to the effect, didn't you hear my take off call out. He replied no he didn't. His tone of voice indicated his unease. I replied calmly I was sorry and that my radio antenna is under the belly of my plane, unstated but, implying that may have been the reason. I continued my departure. If anything like this ever happens again, I will abort the take off even if I had made the radio call out and there is someone, by then, on final behind me. It's a wide runway and I can easily hug it's left side. Previously I had waited at the run up area more than a few times for the airliners to taxi in across Runway 31. I radioed that I am holding in place at the run up area and have them insight. They have always acknowledged my call and say 'thank you.' Additional factor , MTJ isn't completely flat. With my antenna under the belly, it seems it can be a factor for reception for another plane taxiing in along Taxiway A. I think that small aircraft that I didn't fully understand was the business jet. The other thing I will do differently now on is that whenever I hear something that isn't clear, I'll transmit a request for them to repeat it, even if it is a smaller aircraft. I did not give that transmission the importance it deserved because I thought it was an airborne plane piston further away. Also, I should have radioed the business jet to stop prior to crossing Runway 31L missed that during the high stress situation. I was extremely focused on flying the airplane.
ASRSN:2212052.s: The pilot of a piston aircraft at MTJ took off from Runway 31 while a business jet crossed the runway, causing a near-miss. The pilot attributed the incident to poor radio reception due to belly-mounted antennas and terrain, noting the jet did not hear the takeoff callout.

ASRSN:2212054.n: Airport Operations requested to inspect RWY 7L. I put them on the runway and shortly after an aircraft requested to reposition which required a runway crossing. I crossed the aircraft and instructed Operations to pass behind the traffic at Taxiway Echo. The driver did not respond so I reiterated the instruction multiple times. He finally responded with 'okay' but didn't appear to be slowing to I urgently reached out and definitively told the driver to STOP. The driver did not stop and cut off the Aircraft just in front of their nose. The aircraft appeared to slow down and give way to the vehicle.I have experienced a lot of vehicles, both in movement and non movement areas, cut off aircraft recently. I have had pilots call me on Ground to inform me of just having been cut off by a truck, tug, baggage cart, etc. This airport also consistently has trouble with vehicles not operating correctly in regards to closed runways. This driver, for instance, proceeded on a runway that they thought to be closed, without calling Tower, when the runway hadn't even been coordinated as closed from Airport Ops.This airport also has a very high frequency of runway inspections and runway convenience crossings. Often, 3 separate entities, Electricians, Ops, and Maintenance, will inspect the same runway at different times over the course of an hour. Every vehicle operating on a runway introduces risk and the airport should take opportunities to consolidate work to mitigate that risk.
ASRSN:2212054.s: An Air Traffic Controller directed an Airport Operations vehicle to hold behind an aircraft crossing Runway 7L, but the driver ignored instructions and cut off the aircraft. The reporter attributes the incident to the driver entering a runway without coordination and notes a systemic issue of frequent, unconsolidated vehicle inspections increasing risk.

ASRSN:2212055.n: DCA has been suspended from using Pilot Applied and Tower Applied Visual Separation per 7110.65AA. There is already a TFR and a NOTAM in place which are directly conflicting as they restrict different parts from helicopters in close proximity to the airport. The suspension of visual separation went into effect, introduced complexity while introducing risk to DCA and PCT TRACON. Aircraft X was being held approximately 3 miles west of DCA as we are required to provide radar separation between helicopters and fixed wing aircraft in a Class B airspace (1.5 miles or 500 feet). Aircraft X reported that he was minimum fuel while waiting for a gap in the arrivals to be able to proceed back to DCA. Aircraft Y was roughly 3.5 miles south of the field on a visual approach and already cleared to land when I gave him go-around instructions to climb and maintain 3000 feet, turn left heading of 280 in accordance with DCA and PCT's LOA (Letter of Agreement) for go-around procedures. Aircraft Z was approximately 5 miles behind Aircraft Y on a visual approach, also already cleared to land when I also issued a go-around instruction to climb and maintain 3000 feet. Coordination was done at the assistant Local Control position with the Final Controller who was already inundated with other arrivals behind Aircraft Z and an aircraft who was doing checks nearby only adding to the already complex and busy operation at PCT. I told Aircraft Z to continue with his present heading until further advised to not turn him directly towards the Aircraft Y and then issued Aircraft Z the 280 heading when he was already well above Aircraft X and past the point where he would be in direct conflict with Aircraft Y.Recommendation: Allow controllers to use the tools that are prescribed within the 7110.65 as it is the way we are trained to work at a VFR Tower. We are being forced to use minimum radar separation rules while only having a Radar Qualification CBI (Computer Based Instruction) that I had years ago at a different VFR Tower that also had a different class of airspace.
ASRSN:2212055.s: An air traffic controller at DCA issued go-around instructions to two fixed-wing aircraft on visual approach due to a suspension of visual separation and conflicting TFRs. The controller managed the resulting complexity by sequencing the aircraft to avoid conflict with a minimum fuel aircraft held nearby, recommending the restoration of standard visual separation tools.

ASRSN:2212060.n: The airport recently upgraded our airfield lighting panel and there were numerous changes to what the buttons do. An airport operations person called asking about if a specific section of lighting was turned on or not as he was troubleshooting why it wasn't working. I realized it was turned off because on the old panel you would turn the circuits controlling reverse high-speed turn off since they aren't used. The old panel also made it very clear which sections were on and off. The new panel depicts runways and taxiways much smaller and it is more difficult to tell which centerline light sections are on and off. We did not receive any training or an explanation of what changed with the new panel and no one knows exactly what buttons turn what sections on or off.We were not given an opportunity to provide input (that I'm aware of) when the airport was installing and adjusting the panel settings. At a minimum we should get a quick briefing of the changes and know that the reverse high speeds must always be on because they are tied to centerline lighting that leads to the full length of the runway. If you turn them off, a pilot might turn to Taxiway F or M and depart at the intersection because the centerline lights are not on full length.
ASRSN:2212060.s: Airport operations personnel and the reporter identified that a new airfield lighting panel caused confusion due to unclear indicators and lack of training. Turning off reverse high-speed circuits inadvertently disabled full-length centerline lighting, creating a risk that pilots could depart from an intersection without proper visual guidance.

ASRSN:2212063.n: When we got in at XA:30 the Controller in Charge (CIC) told us that Traffic Management Unit (TMU) had advised them that LAS would be busy until XD:00, but that's all the info/help we got. The closing coworkers had combined all 5 sectors up before XB:30 and around XB:45. I came back from break and de-combined sectors 54/55 to one scope and my mid partner was working 06/16/34 combined on the other scope. No one could stay to help because they were all already on 10-hour days and off at XA:00. Starting around that time, approximately Day 0 XA:00, I started to get a large number of LAS arrivals on the east side of the complex, while the west side (06/16) was getting spun and put into and out of holding. I had over 25 aircraft landing LAS within a 120-mile radius on 3 different arrival streams, two from ZLC and one from ZDV. TMU told me before they went home that they told ZDV to give us 15 MIT but that was zero help considering the volume I was receiving from all 3 flows. This barrage of arrivals continued on for an hour. There was literally nowhere to put all these aircraft. At one point I turned to my coworker and told him that I was at a loss, I have no idea what to do with all these aircraft there is literally nowhere to put them. My coworker then ended up calling the surrounding centers for me and choosing some aircraft to spin because I didn't have a spare second to go on the line.To add to this complexity, there were bad rides, some minimal weather and still overflights and departure traffic. The frequency congestion was filled with aircraft with lengthy ride reports and questions, aircraft checking in on my frequency in error since the surrounding sectors weren't used to us being de-combined so late, and I had one aircraft requesting a deviation for a buildup. They were getting moderate chop between FL260 and FL360 throughout my sector. The area controller who was working sectors 7/8/35/36 combined (these sectors surround our sectors) was too busy to use CPDLC so I had to 'steal eligibility' on ALL the CPDLC aircraft which added even more tasks to do. This controller was also working both east arrival flows alone.Management was well aware of what was coming and did nothing besides tell the two of us to 'make sure we stay de-combined;' apparently trying to check their box off, they told us not to combine up. Despite staying de-combined, the sector was unmanageable and unworkable. Both my mid partner and I have years of experience at ZLA and neither of us have ever seen something like this, that late at night with no staffing or help.After speaking with coworkers who were on the day shift, there was a ground stop during the day for LAS multiple times, and LAS stayed at a very low arrival rate of 36 all day long and config 1. There were no deviations on the day shift but they were still spun twice despite the low arrival rate. Sounds like the airport was slowed down all day long 'just in case' and then everyone goes home at XB:30 and everyone on the ground takes off at once. What I experienced last night was incredibly dangerous, and I do not say that lightly. If this had happened to two more inexperienced controllers, who knows what the outcome would've been. We are told during these countless safety briefings to just refuse handoffs or spin aircraft when we're overloaded, this is also an illogical response as now we're just pushing off the busy workload on other people. Salt Lake Center had conflict alert going off between multiple of these aircraft as they were trying to spin 4 - 5 of these arrivals for me as well as working their own busy traffic (yesterday was extremely high volume overall). It is completely unacceptable for there to be a ground stop and very low arrival rate all day and then after XB:30 everyone goes home and everyone on the ground takes off at once. It's illogical and dangerous. I want to say that I can't believe this happened, but I can. During safety briefings we're just told to push off aninsane workload on the previous controller who is also busy, when the actual solution should be that all these aircraft should NOT have been in the air AT THE SAME TIME. There were minimal arrivals to LAS after XD:15, why were these 100 aircraft not spread out over the nighttime hours? When I came back to work from XG:00 - XJ:00, I had TWO arrivals to LAS. There is no reason that these air carriers should've all been allowed to depart all at once just to keep their passengers happy. As far as I can tell, absolutely nothing was done to mitigate the situation besides telling me and my coworker we were 'gonna be busy' and then trying to give MIT on one of 7 arrival streams. With staffing already at desperate levels and getting worse and worse with losing people and the terrible new schedule rules, we need something that staggers these arrivals all night. The old way of 'TMU went home, you're all on your own' is NOT going to work anymore and something safety related is going to happen eventually. I know LAS isn't the only airport with this issue, this goes for any airport that's delayed all day and then all delays lifted at XC:00.
ASRSN:2212063.s: Two experienced air traffic controllers at Salt Lake Center faced an unmanageable workload during a late-night surge of over 25 LAS arrivals after a ground stop was lifted. The reporter attributes the dangerous situation to poor traffic flow management that released all delayed aircraft simultaneously without adequate staffing or mitigation.

ASRSN:2212075.n: Aircraft X was doing a procedure turn at KENIR to do the ILS 20 approach into PGV. The weather from the previous controller, and myself, was called multiple times. Moderate to Severe precipitation was moving across the localizer. Aircraft X finished the procedure turn and was approaching final when I called the weather again. I told the pilot to stay with me until he felt safe to start his approach. Aircraft X said they were ready and I switched him to advisories. I began working my other traffic and calling the precipitation to other aircraft.Aircraft X called back out of five thousand two hundred feet, which is well above the published missed approach of one thousand six hundred. Aircraft X said they had to abort the landing and had to climb above the weather. Aircraft X declared severe turbulence with 700 ft loss and wind shear of +/- 40 knots. I climbed Aircraft X to 060. Aircraft X declared they wanted to return to ZZZ. I assigned a safe heading away from the weather and traffic and climbed them to FL200. I gave them their clearance to return to ZZZ with a deviation to get around the precipitation. I asked if they had any structural or injuries from the severe turbulence. They responded in the negative. Afterwards, I assume they discovered some structural damage and reported it to Atlanta Center.I do not think this event could have been avoided. All weather was called, the pilot wanted to attempt the approach. Once the wind shear was felt, the pilot correctly aborted the approach. All IFR traffic was separated and safe. Aircraft X checked in from sector 27 destined for PGV @ fl230. I informed the pilot of moderate through extreme precipitation along their route to the PGV airport. After a discussion about which approach they wanted, I issued a clearance direct to the initial approach fix with a pilot's discretion descent. The pilot informed me that they were unable to obtain ceiling information so I offered them the ceiling from the weather reports from either MCZ or ISO. the pilot opted for ZZZ1. I informed the OS (Operations Supervisor) that the weather report was missing from the PGV observation and he called it in to Maintenance. After clearing Aircraft X for the ILS 20, Aircraft X requested a left turn just prior to KENIR (the IAF) to continue their descent and I 'approved' the request. After approving the request, I gave a position relief briefing and left the control room. After getting back in to the control room and receiving a briefing for the CIC position, I was informed that Aircraft X encountered severe turbulence on their approach and returned to ZZZ. shortly thereafter, I was informed that Aircraft X reported damage to ZZZ Center.
ASRSN:2212075.s: Air Traffic Controllers warned Aircraft X of severe precipitation during an ILS 20 approach to PGV. The pilot encountered wind shear and turbulence, lost 700 feet, aborted the landing, and later reported structural damage while returning to ZZZ.

ASRSN:2212108.n: After arrival at destination a deadheading pilot stopped by the cockpit to show us photos of the leading edge sheet metal panel inboard of the left engine. Five rivets in a row appeared to be missing causing the panel to bow up at the location of the five rivets. After landing the panel returned to its flush position with no evidence of any problems. I notified MX via Electronic Log Book (ELB) and spoke with Maintenance Control. The technitions climbed up on the wing and could not find any problems. After showing the the photos of the bow in flight it was discovered the the rivets were still in place but the rivet heads had pulled through the sheet metal. Without the inflight photo evidence, this problem would most likely be difficult for maintenance to discover without taking the wing apart. The problem rivets, while still in place, were hidden from below by the LE heat duct. The aircraft was removed from service and we took a delay waiting on an inbound aircraft to fly our return flight to ZZZ. This makes me wonder how many other rivets may be exhibiting similar behavior but go unnoticed.
ASRSN:2212108.s: A deadheading pilot reported missing rivets on the left engine leading edge panel after arrival, but maintenance found the rivet heads had pulled through the sheet metal, hidden by the heat duct. The aircraft was removed from service for repairs, causing a delay while waiting for a replacement to return to ZZZ.

ASRSN:2212111.n: During engine start the EICAS 'OVERHEAT ENG R' WITH CHECKLIST ICON appeared. The right EGT was slightly higher by only 20 degrees or so. The Overheat EICAS was coming on and off. First Officer (FO) began to run the checklist then the FIRE INDICATIONS on the right engine started (bell+lights). Engine was secured and fire handle pulled but light went out so no bottles were discharged. Crew called ramp on XXX.XXX to have the fire department come and inspect the right engine. I don't recall if the FO actually advised ATC at that time as I was helping the Captain deal with the checklists/actions. Over 10-15 minutes passed before any emergency vehicles showed up. Responders found nothing of concern so we hooked up to a tug and towed back into gate XX at XA:00. Gate agents were prompt arriving at the jetway and opening the cabin door. Passengers remained onboard while maintenance inspected the aircraft. Ultimately the flight cancelled but the cancellation determination took nearly 2 hours. Crew reviewed required reporting Items: Dispatch notified, chief pilot briefed, reports made.
ASRSN:2212111.s: During engine start, the crew secured the right engine after intermittent overheat and fire indications, though no fire bottles were discharged. Emergency responders found no issues, but the flight was cancelled following a two-hour maintenance inspection while passengers remained onboard.

ASRSN:2212139.n: After departure from the Gate, we taxied to the Runway and sent a message. The FO called Ops. Several minutes later, Ops called back to report that dry ice loaded as DG had the wrong number of parcels in the two cargo compartments. We were directed to return to a parking stand and ground personnel moved the DG as required. A new DG message was received and acknowledged. Messaging was accomplished with Dispatch via ACARS. The flight departed and arrived late due to this delay, but there were no other operation impacts. I am reporting as directed in FOM. After departure from the gate, we taxied to the Runway and sent a message. The FO called Ops. Several minutes later, Ops called back to report that dry ice loaded as DG had the wrong number of parcels in the two cargo compartments. We were directed to return to a parking stand and ground personnel moved the DG as required. A new DG message was received and acknowledged. Messaging was accomplished with Dispatch via ACARS. The flight departed and arrived late due to this delay, but there were no other operation impacts. I am reporting as recommended in FOM.
